title: WHY DID GOD CALL SOME ANIMALS CLEAN—AND OTHERS UNCLEAN?
paragraphs: WHY DID GOD CALL SOME ANIMALS CLEAN—AND OTHERS UNCLEAN?

The strange food laws of Leviticus were never merely about what was on Israel’s plate. They were teaching a holy people how to recognize the difference between what God sets apart and what He does not—and they ultimately drive us toward a much deeper question: What can actually make an unclean sinner clean?
There is something unsettling about Leviticus 11.
Not because it is difficult to read.
Certain fish could be eaten. Others could not.
Some birds belonged on Israel’s table. Others were forbidden.
Even creatures that crawled along the ground were classified.
And somewhere between the divided hoof, the chewing of the cud, fins, scales, birds, insects, and creeping things, a modern reader can understandably stop and ask:
Why would the God who created every animal call some “clean” and others “unclean”?
Was God saying pigs were evil?
Was this merely an ancient health code disguised as religion?
And perhaps the question underneath all the others is even more important:
If God cared so much about these distinctions then, why do Christians today eat foods that Israel was commanded not to eat?
Because what begins with animals eventually reaches the human heart.
And when it does, Leviticus stops feeling like an ancient dietary manual.
It starts feeling like a mirror.
Long before Moses stood before Israel, Scripture already used the distinction between clean and unclean animals.
Before the Mosaic covenant was formally given.
When Noah entered the ark, Genesis 7:2 distinguishes between animals described in Hebrew as הַבְּהֵמָה הַטְּהוֹרָה—ha-behemah ha-tehorah, “the clean animal”—and animals “that are not clean.”
So the concept did not suddenly appear in Leviticus.
But at Sinai, God incorporated these distinctions into Israel’s covenant life with extraordinary detail.

Leviticus 11 describes land animals Israel could eat as those possessing particular characteristics, including divided hooves and chewing the cud. Aquatic creatures needed fins and scales. The chapter also identifies prohibited birds and distinguishes among insects and other creatures.
But if we stop at the menu, we miss the sermon.
Near the end of the chapter, God reveals something much deeper:
כִּי אֲנִי יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם וְהִתְקַדִּשְׁתֶּם וִהְיִיתֶם קְדֹשִׁים כִּי קָדוֹשׁ אָנִי
Ki ani YHWH Eloheikhem, vehitqaddishtem vihyitem qedoshim, ki qadosh ani.
“For I am the LORD your God. Consecrate yourselves and be holy, because I am holy.”
The Hebrew word קָדוֹשׁ—qadosh—carries the idea of holiness, of being set apart.
God was forming Israel into a people who belonged uniquely to Him.
Their covenant signs would be different.
Their relationship with the nations would be different.
Even ordinary moments around a dinner table could remind them:
You wake up in the morning.
Israel could not conveniently confine the LORD to a religious ceremony and then live the remainder of life as though He did not exist.
The covenant reached into ordinary existence.
That was part of the point.
And Scripture itself explicitly connects Israel’s animal distinctions with Israel’s own distinction from the nations.
Leviticus 20 tells Israel to distinguish between clean and unclean animals and then immediately reminds them that God had set Israel apart from other peoples to belong to Him.
Then He taught His separated people to live with separation woven into the rhythms of everyday life.
Not because creation itself was somehow evil.
Genesis had already declared God’s creation good.
Rather, within Israel’s covenant, God designated creatures differently for particular purposes and taught His people to recognize His distinctions.
Leviticus 11:47 gives the purpose with remarkable clarity:
“To distinguish between the unclean and the clean.”
The Hebrew verb lehavdil carries the idea of separating or distinguishing.
Human preference does not overrule divine revelation.
That lesson reaches far beyond dinner.
And this is where we should be careful with explanations that sound convincing but go beyond Scripture.
You may have heard that the forbidden animals were prohibited simply because they were unhealthy, carried more disease, were scavengers, or were medically dangerous.
Some proposed explanations may contain observations worth discussing.
But the Bible itself does not tell us that disease prevention was the comprehensive reason for the classifications.
So we should not pretend God explained something He did not explain.

These regulations belonged to Israel’s covenant life and were explicitly associated with holiness, distinction, obedience, and Israel’s identity as a people belonging to God. Deuteronomy similarly places dietary instructions alongside the declaration that Israel was a holy people chosen as God’s treasured possession.
And suddenly the dinner table becomes a classroom.
And everything moves toward something deeper.
In Mark 7, Jesus is confronting a controversy concerning defilement.
And He moves the conversation from the outside...
To what comes out of a person.
The Greek text of Mark 7:19 contains the striking expression:
“cleansing/declaring clean all foods,” reflected in many modern translations as Jesus declaring all foods clean.
But then Jesus says something considerably more frightening than anything about pork.
What truly defiles a human being comes from within.
And now the knife turns toward us.
Because it is easy to stand over Leviticus 11 asking:
It is considerably harder to stand before Mark 7 asking:
We like external religion because external religion can sometimes be managed.
Know when to raise your hands.
But Jesus walks past appearances and goes straight into the room we hoped nobody would enter.
That resentment you have been feeding.
That affair beginning inside your imagination.
That secret message you keep deleting.
That pride disguised as spiritual maturity.
That hatred you justify because the other person hurt you first.
That hidden version of you that appears when the church people are gone.
And suddenly the ancient language of clean and unclean becomes painfully personal.
Because humanity’s deepest problem has never been that we accidentally touched the wrong animal.
We have not merely violated dietary boundaries.
We have violated the holiness of God.
And things we should have done but refused to do.
The scandal is not simply that something outside us might be unclean.
The scandal is that sin has come from within us.
And no amount of religious cosmetics can wash it away.
But this is exactly where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Jesus Christ did not come merely to make bad people slightly more respectable.
The Holy One walked among the unclean.
He ate with people respectable religion preferred to keep at a distance.
Yet He did not become morally contaminated by their sin.
Instead, holiness moved toward the unclean.
And eventually Jesus walked toward a cross.
The One without sin was treated as condemned.
The spotless Lamb shed His blood.
Not because our sin was insignificant.
Because it was so serious that redemption cost blood.
The Gospel is not God pretending you were always clean.
The Gospel is God confronting the full horror of our sin and providing cleansing through Christ.
You do not cleanse yourself and then approach Jesus.
You approach Jesus because you cannot cleanse yourself.
Maybe that is what someone reading this desperately needs to hear.
You have been hiding because you believe Jesus only welcomes the already-clean.
But if sinners could make themselves clean enough to deserve God, Calvary would have been unnecessary.
You do not need a better disguise.
Then Acts 10 gives us one of the most dramatic moments in this entire biblical storyline.
A sheet descends containing various animals.
A voice tells him to rise, kill, and eat.
Peter protests that he has never eaten anything koinon kai akatharton—“common and unclean.”
Ἃ ὁ Θεὸς ἐκαθάρισεν σὺ μὴ κοίνου
Ha ho Theos ekatharisen, sy mē koinou.
“What God has cleansed, you must not call common.”
But we must not rip the vision away from its own inspired interpretation.
Peter later explains what God showed him:
κἀμοὶ ὁ θεὸς ἔδειξεν μηδένα κοινὸν ἢ ἀκάθαρτον λέγειν ἄνθρωπον
God had shown him not to call any person common or unclean.
The Gospel was breaking through barriers.
The good news of Jesus Christ was not a private possession for one ethnicity.
Christ's kingdom would gather people from the nations.
A Jewish man shaped by a lifetime of boundaries.
Then God sends him through the doorway of a Gentile home.
And the Gospel walks in with him.
People whom Peter might once have regarded as outside were hearing the Gospel.
And this is why Christians must be cautious about turning food into a basis for spiritual superiority.
Nothing is “common” or unclean in itself, while he also commands believers to take conscience and love for one another seriously.
Paul likewise warns Christians not to allow others to judge them regarding food and drink in Colossians 2:16.
“For every creation of God is good...”
and is to be received with thanksgiving.
That does not mean Christians should become careless about health, gluttony, conscience, stewardship, or loving fellow believers.
Christian freedom is never permission for selfishness.
But the New Testament does not place Gentile believers under Israel’s Levitical dietary code as the means by which they become holy before God.
Our standing before God is not produced by the contents of our refrigerator.
And maybe now we can finally see why this seemingly strange chapter matters so much.
God determines what is clean and unclean.
Sin and impurity cannot simply be shrugged away.
And the Gospel eventually reveals the astonishing answer to the problem those categories force us to confront:
How can the unclean become clean?
Not your ability to hide what happened.
Not your promise that you will “do better this time.”
The blood of Christ reaches places human religion cannot reach.
And perhaps you have spent years trying to appear clean while quietly bleeding inside.
People see the Sunday version of you.
God hears what you tell yourself when the room is empty.
God sees the wound beneath it.
Repentance does not mean pretending the stain never happened.
It means bringing the truth into the light and turning toward Christ.
Grace does not tell you sin was acceptable.
Grace tells you sin does not have to have the final word.
Someone else reading those words may realize they are not the only person fighting their way back toward the light.
Do not keep this article trapped on your screen.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
Send this privately to the person who thinks they have become too dirty for Jesus.

Scripture explicitly teaches Christian generosity without coercion: giving is to come from a willing heart rather than compulsion.
But voluntary financial support can still become a meaningful way of participating in Gospel ministry.
One share can put Scripture in front of someone we could never personally reach.
One tag can begin a conversation.
One saved article can be rediscovered on the night somebody desperately needs it.
One honest comment can give another struggling believer permission to stop pretending.

never confuse supporting a ministry with purchasing God's favor.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
So give freely if God has put generosity in your heart.
Share freely if this truth could help someone.
Follow if you want to keep growing.
Because perhaps the most haunting lesson hidden inside the ancient distinction between clean and unclean is not that God once cared deeply about what Israel placed on the table.
It is that the holy God has always had the right to define holiness.
And when we discovered that we could never make ourselves clean enough to stand before Him...
the Holy One came looking for the unclean.
